content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper proposes to train an ensemble of LMs based on some labeled division of the dataset. 

The paper proposes to train different LMs on different domains and merge them as a model ensemble. 

Reviewers recognized that the paper contains extensive experimental efforts. However, concerns are raised about the fairness of the experiments (which was not addressed in the author response). Moreover, reviewers find that model ensemble does not seem to be novel.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Lack of novelty and unfair comparison.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting:
We had a virtual meeting on Nov 28. Reviewers mentioned that the paper is well-written and well-crafted. However, reviewers re-iterated that the approach is not novel (and somewhat trivial), and that experiments are not fair (which was not responded by authors). 

Being well-written and well-crafted is a necessary condition of acceptance. It does not justify the acceptance by itself.

This is not limiting to applicability but important to have.

content.title: Response to Reviewer B2er
content.comment:
***Reviewer B2er.*** We thank reviewer B2er for their time and their comments. We respond to their review below:

**Motivation for branching** ("issues still remain unknown and insights behind this design is also lacking... why the model need to branch from some LMs on the similar domains? "). From our response to reviewer uT5X: We cite several inspirations in the paper (Section 2, Section 6), a few of which we briefly summarized here: The inspiration for sparse activation via separate models as experts comes from MoE models, especially early versions (Jacobs et al., 1991). The idea of using data domain to specialize model parameters was previously executed with success by Gururangan et. al (2022), which trains domain-expert layers. Prior work investigates the necessity of partially shared optimization trajectories for parameter averaging, and of gradual sparsification, which are related to our branching and merging procedures (Frankle et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2021). Our work is partially motivated by these and other existing literature.

**Explanation for domain data splits improving performance over random splits** ("Why does the merging of models trained on different domains lead to better performance rather than the models trained on random splits?"). Previous work [1,2] has suggested that in certain regimes, linear combinations of neural network weights approximate ensembling their outputs. Indeed, we observe strong correlations between the performance of averaging and ensembling in Figure 2. As we note in Footnote 6, we hypothesize that output ensembles with random splits tend to make correlated errors [3], contributing to their worse performance. However, what level of specialization is necessary for model merging to work is not known yet, and is a ripe area for future work. 

**Downstream task performance** ("The trained LLMs are not evaluated on the downstream tasks."). From our response to reviewer uT5X: We omit downstream task evaluations in our paper. Instead, our work intentionally focuses on improving language modeling performance. Advances in language modeling have smoothly translated into equally substantial improvements on downstream tasks (see recent LM work, e.g., Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022, cited in our work). Thus, our paper, while explicitly scoped to language modeling, is not limited in applicability, though we do leave the explicit measurement of downstream effects for future work.

**Designing pre-training explicitly for parameter averages** ("pre-training design based on weights merging is still under explored"). We agree that there may be other, possibly higher-performing ways to conduct BTM training for best parameter-averaging inference results. We do not claim optimality; in this work, we introduce this procedure, demonstrate its viability, then ablate and analyse a few variations, but are limited by the scoping of a single paper. We hope to study the impact of further variations in the training procedure on both ensembling and averaging inference in future work.

[1]  Wortsman, Mitchell, et al. Model soups: averaging weights of multiple fine-tuned models improves accuracy without increasing inference time. ICML, 2022
[2] Wortsman, Mitchell, et al. Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models. CVPR, 2022.
[3] Gontijo-Lopes et al., No one representation to rule them all: Overlapping features of training methods. ICLR, 2022

content.title: Response to Reviewer uT5X
content.comment:
***Reviewer uT5X.*** We thank reviewer uT5X for their time and their comments. We respond to their review below:

**Downstream task performance** ("work would be more complete to have the results on other downstream tasks"). We omit downstream task evaluations in our paper. Instead, our work intentionally focuses on improving language modeling performance. Advances in language modeling have smoothly translated into equally substantial improvements on downstream tasks (see recent LM work, e.g., Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022, cited in our work). Thus, our paper, while explicitly scoped to language modeling, is not limited in applicability, though we do leave the explicit measurement of downstream effects for future work.

**Motivation for branching** ("motivation is unclear … Why do you choose to branch the LMs? How can they be effective?"). We cite several inspirations in the paper (Section 2, Section 6), a few of which we briefly summarized here: The inspiration for sparse activation via separate models as experts comes from MoE models, especially early versions (Jacobs et al., 1991). The idea of using data domain to specialize model parameters was previously executed with success by Gururangan et. al (2022), which trains domain-expert layers. Prior work investigates the necessity of partially shared optimization trajectories for parameter averaging, and of gradual sparsification, which are related to our branching and merging procedures (Frankle et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2021). Our work is partially motivated by these and other existing literature.

**Additional experiments showing variance** ("authors only show the standard deviation on the smallest model. Can you also put the number on larger models?"). We show standard deviations on 8 random seeds for our smallest scale experiments. Performing experiments for each of the 3 larger setups at 8 random seeds would result in expenditure of roughly 10,000 GPU-days. There were only small variances in performance across random seeds at the 125M parameter scale, especially on our proposed BTM method; thus, we did not find it worth the resource (or financial and environmental) cost to measure variance at the larger scale. We can add text clarifying this rationale.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Rw95
content.comment:
***Reviewer Rw95.*** We thank reviewer Rw95 for their time and their comments. We respond to their review below:

**Inference cost and assumptions** (" the inference cost can be very high if we want to gain good performance … the paper proposed using domain posterior to activate only related trained experts. The assumption is not used in other models, so it seems unfair.") As stated clearly in Section 2.2, our inference process does use a sample of data from the target distribution to calculate mixture weights. We agree that this constitutes a difference in inference procedure between our method and the baseline Transformer LM. In Gururangan et. al, 2022, the DEMix baseline is compared to a “domain token” baseline, where the dense language model is trained with a string prefix that indicates the domain of the target document, and these domain tokens are presented to the model at evaluation time as well. It was found that while domain token baseline was comparable to DEMix with respect to in-domain performance, it fails on out-of-domain text. As our model outperforms DEMix, we expect to see the same trends in this work, and will add this point as discussion.  Regarding the difference in inference costs, our averaging procedure, which outperforms all baselines, is inference-compute-matched to the densely-trained single Transformer LM baseline, which it outperforms. Our ensembling procedure requires additional inference compute over the baseline Transformer LM, in the form of parallelizable forward passes through multiple experts. However, as stated in the response to kH7N, we see empirically that only 2-3 experts need to be activated, rather than all 8. Thus, we provide 2 modes of inference which both outperform the baseline Transformer LM, and offer to users an accuracy-compute tradeoff choice at inference time (see Section 4.4 for details).

content.title: Response to Reviewer kH7N
content.comment:
***Reviewer kH7N.*** We thank reviewer kH7N for their time and their comments. We respond to their review below:

**Novelty of ensembling** ("ensemble of many deep learning models is a well-known idea … highlight the difference between your work and previous works"). Our paper does not claim to describe a new algorithm for combining model outputs in an ensemble. However, we do introduce a novel training method which results in a set of domain-specific experts which can be ensembled. Succinctly, some differences between our paper and an ensembling paper are: (1) vanilla ensembling does not partition the data into domains in order to train separate models, which is essential for our efficiently embarrassingly parallel training (2) the vanilla ensembling approach we compare against in Table 4 and Appendix Table 10 underperforms our method, as well as the densely-trained baseline Transformer LM, and (3) ensembling is not the only inference mode available to our ELMforests since we also demonstrate the efficacy of parameter averaging (Section 4.4).

**Additional parameter-matched baseline** ("more meaningful experiment is to compare the accuracy of the ELM model with a Transformer-LM with the same number of parameters and check whether the ELM model can match the performance"). Our models are intentionally compute-matched rather than parameter-matched, as compute budget is typically the limiting factor. This is in line with the current literature studying sparse LMs (see Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022; Lewis et al., 2021; Roller et al., 2021; Gururangan et al., 2022, etc., cited in our work). Additionally, in our parameter averaging results, our final model for each evaluation domain is parameter matched to the baseline densely-trained Transformer LMs. We show in Section 4.4 that this parameter-matched but more efficient to train ELMForest outperforms the densely trained Transformer baseline.

**Additional ensemble using the baseline Transformer LM** ("ensemble the baseline Transformer-LM across different checkpoints and this can also boost the final inference performance. How does this baseline compare with the proposed method?"). In our Random Ensemble setting, we ensemble many different baseline Transformer LMs. This setting underperforms our ELMforest models, as seen in Table 4 and Appendix Table 10. We didn’t try checkpoint averaging, e.g. as commonly used for the last few checkpoints in NMT, but it is orthogonal to our techniques and will almost certainly help both the dense models and individual ELMs; this would be interesting to explore in future work. 

**More details on inference speed** ("only provides the per-step speed during training … provide a more detailed study on the convergence/inference speed of the expert-based LM"). Inference speed per expert is identical to that of the baseline Transformer LM, as the architectures are matched, and the forward pass activates each parameter within one expert. Thus, if all experts are activated (as we do naively), inference wall-clock time can be identical, but compute cost is multiplied by the number of experts. Empirically, we find that expert activation weights are sparse, and that activating only 2 or 3 experts, instead of all 8, does not change performance, which could lead to more work on efficient inference in the future, and we would be happy to add this to the discussion. Finally, our parameter averaging results reduce the ELMforest to a single model, and therefore have the same inference cost as the baseline Transformer LM.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper propose a new LM architecture that trains branches of LMs on different dataset domains and ensemble the results by taking a weighted average of the output logits or the model parameters. Adding a new LM branch can be done by first taking a weighted average over the existing weights, and then training on the new domain.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper proposes a promising modification to the current LLM training scheme. Specifically, I found the way the authors combine the outputs with domain posterior interesting. However, I have the following concerns regarding the proposed method and its evaluation:

- The technique of ensemble of many deep learning models is a well-known idea in deep learning. The paper uses a standard ensemble method with limited algorithmic innovations. Please highlight the difference between your work and previous works on
- The results in Table 1 are not fair because different models have different numbers of parameters. A more meaningful experiment is to compare the accuracy of the ELM model with a Transformer-LM with the same number of parameters and check whether the ELM model can match the performance with less training cost, or can outperform Transformer-LM under the same training budget.
- In addition, one can also ensemble the baseline Transformer-LM across different checkpoints and this can also boost the final inference performance. How does this baseline compare with the proposed method?
- The study on the speed/efficiency of the proposed method is not complete. Table 2 only provides the per-step speed during training. Please provide a more detailed study on the convergence/inference speed of the expert-based LM.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and easy to understand. The result should be able to be reproduced with the code provided. However, I do have concerns on the novelty of the paper as indicated above.
content.summary_of_the_review: I have concerns about the novelty of the work and the experiments to evaluate the proposed idea.

The paper introduces BTM training, a new algorithm to train an ELMForest, which contains many expert LMs that can be ensembled or parameter averaged at any time for efficient training and rapid customization.

Strength
1. The experiments are very extensive, the ELMforest ensembles outperform baselines at no additional training cost.

Weekness
1. The evaluation for the parameter averaged ELMforests seems not fair, given that during evaluation the parameter averaged model can activate domain related experts on the test set. The hidden assumption is that the consecutive sentences in the test set are from the same domain. 
2. If the parameter average approach doesn't give reasonable performance, the inference cost can be very high if we want to gain good performance.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces BTM training to train a collection of Expert LMs that built an ELMFOREST. Each component in the forest can be dynamically added/removed/ensembled (merged) at any time. The idea of the method is to train scalable and parallel individual models that each specialize in a particular domain. The paper presents comprehensive experiments and analyses. The study improves in- and out-of-domain perplexities as compared to GPT-style transformer LMs.

Main contributions:
- Propose a new framework to efficiently train language models
- Evaluate the proposed method on various datasets (in- and out-domains)
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
-  Interesting approach of learning models in parallel and running on multi-node. The paper introduces a new learning framework to train multiple models on different domains and merge them.

**Weaknesses:**
- The evaluation is limited to language model perplexity. The work would be more complete to have the results on other downstream tasks. Did you have any chance to evaluate the model on downstream NLP tasks? And does the model have the same capability as standard GPT models (i.e., in-context learning or generation tasks)?
- The motivation is unclear on why the authors proposed to branch-train-and merge. Why do you choose to branch the LMs? How can they be effective?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:**
- The paper is well-written and the method is clear. 
- Missing details: On Table 1, the authors only show the standard deviation on the smallest model. Can you also put the number on larger models? and did you run on 8 different seeds as well?

**Quality:**
- The writing is good. No critical typographical issues.

**Novelty:**
- The proposed method has novel ideas to branch and grow a forest by training models. 

**Reproducibility:**
- The authors plan to release the code.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper has new ideas for learning efficient language models in a parallel and non-synchronized manner. And the proposed method can be effectively used to build language models via ensemble.

I would gladly see the paper at the conference and give a "marginally above the acceptance threshold" score. However, there are some questions and concerns, and I will adjust the score if the authors address my concerns.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper is on build language models via embarrassingly parallel training mechanism. More specifically, the author propose a branch train and merge method, which could build the large-scale language models by independently training subparts of a new class of LLMs on different subsets of the data. Such a way is able to eliminate the massive multi-node synchronization currently required to train LLMs. The results show that this training paradigm could be used to efficiently scale LLMs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The studied topic is at the core of community's interest. How to scale the large scale language models  with reduced costs is important for many tasks. The branch, train and merge framework has a clear design and the empirical studies supported the design idea and indicate the problems that the authors has faced. The proposed method is validated on the large scale datasets and suggest the effectiveness of the paradigm.

Weakness:
1. Some of issues still remain unknown and insights behind this design is also lacking. For example, why the model need to branch from some LMs on the similar domains? Why does the merging of models trained on different domains lead to better performance rather than the models trained on random splits?
2. The trained LLMs are not evaluated on the downstream tasks. The evaluation of downstream tasks are useful to understand the effectiveness of this training paradigm. GPT style models usually have strong few-shot abilities and strong generation abilities. Look forward to seeing the corresponding results to support the effectiveness claims.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and easy to follow.
The paper has its merits and shows important findings. However, some findings will be more valuable if insights and hypothesis behind the findings could be provided.
The novelty is clearly shown. Even thought merging the weights of pre-trained model is explored, the pre-training design based on weights merging is still under explored. 
The reproducibility could be validated based on the released checkpoints.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors design an elegant and impactful pre-training design, which could potential change the current pre-training mechanism and reduce the training costs. The findings are valuable and will be more impactful if more insights and hypothesis could be provided. The performance on the downstream tasks are missing. The paper quality will be further improved if the downstream task experiments could be added.

content.title: Branch-Train-Merge: Embarrassingly Parallel Training of Expert Language Models
content.TL;DR: We develop a new class of large language models that is embarrassingly parallel: different parts of the model are independently trained on different subsets of the data, with no need for multi-node training or inference.
content.abstract: We present Branch-Train-Merge (BTM), a communication-efficient algorithm for embarrassingly parallel training of large language models (LLMs). We show it is possible to independently train subparts of a new class of LLMs on different subsets of the data, eliminating the massive multi-node synchronization currently required to train LLMs.  BTM learns a set of independent Expert LMs (ELMs), each specialized to a different textual domain, such as scientific or legal text. These ELMs can be added and removed to update data coverage, ensembled to generalize to new domains, or averaged to collapse back to a single LM for efficient inference. New ELMs are  learned by branching from (mixtures of) ELMs in the current set, further training on new domains, and then merging the resulting models back into the set for future use. Experiments show that BTM improves in- and out-of-domain perplexities as compared to GPT-style Transformer LMs, when controlling for training cost. Through extensive analysis, we show that these results are robust to different ELM initialization schemes, but require expert domain specialization; ensembles with random data splits do not perform well. Our results suggest that aggressive parallelism could be used to efficiently scale larger LMs in future work.
